state.description:
Current business state of the todo item.

This is mapped from `todo_app_todos.state`. Typical conceptual values include states such as "active" or "pending" for open tasks and "completed" for finished tasks. Application logic may also treat rows with `deleted_at` set as logically deleted even if `state` still reflects the last visible state.

Clients primarily use this field to render visual indicators and filter or group todos by status in summary lists.

due_date.description:
Optional target date and time by which the user intends to complete the todo.

This field is backed by `todo_app_todos.due_date` and may be null when the todo has no explicit due date. When present, it is an ISO 8601 date-time string in UTC or a well-defined timezone. User interfaces typically surface this in list views to highlight upcoming or overdue tasks.

created_at.description:
Creation timestamp of the todo item.

This field reflects `todo_app_todos.created_at` and captures when the todo was first inserted. It is useful for chronological ordering of todos and for displaying metadata such as "created on" in list or detail views.

updated_at.description:
Timestamp of the most recent modification to this todo.

This value mirrors `todo_app_todos.updated_at` and is updated whenever the todo content or state changes. Client applications can use it to show "last updated" information or to detect that a todo has changed since it was last displayed.

completed_at.description:
Timestamp when the todo was most recently completed, if ever.

This field is mapped from `todo_app_todos.completed_at`. It is null when the todo has never been completed or has been reopened without being completed again. When non-null, it records the exact time the todo entered the completed state and can be used for analytics or history views.

ITodoAppAdminUserSession.IRequest.description:
Search and filter DTO for listing administrative user sessions for the todoApp backend.

This request type is used by the admin session index endpoint to query `todo_app_adminuser_sessions` records belonging to a specific administrative user. It provides pagination controls, optional filtering by creation time, and optional IP address matching to support security monitoring use cases.

The DTO is designed for read-only analytics and dashboards. It never creates or mutates sessions; it only influences how existing session rows are selected and ordered when generating a paginated summary response.

page.description:
Page index for pagination when listing admin user sessions.

Clients generally treat this as a 1-based page number, where `1` represents the first page of results. The server may normalize or clamp invalid values to a sensible default to avoid errors.

limit.description:
Maximum number of session records to return in a single page of results.

This value controls the page size for the query against `todo_app_adminuser_sessions`. Servers should enforce an upper bound to prevent excessively large result sets that could degrade performance.

fromCreatedAt.description:
Optional inclusive lower bound for the `created_at` timestamp of admin user sessions to include in the result set.

When provided, only sessions whose `created_at` value is greater than or equal to this ISO 8601 timestamp are considered. Use this together with `toCreatedAt` for time-range based investigations.

toCreatedAt.description:
Optional inclusive upper bound for the `created_at` timestamp of admin user sessions to include in the result set.

When provided, only sessions whose `created_at` value is less than or equal to this ISO 8601 timestamp are considered. Use this together with `fromCreatedAt` for bounded time-window queries.

ip.description:
Optional filter for matching the `ip` column of `todo_app_adminuser_sessions`.

When specified, only sessions whose stored IP address matches this value are returned. This is useful for tracing activity from a specific administrative workstation or network location.

oneOf.description:
Sorting direction for the `created_at` field when ordering admin user sessions in ascending chronological order (oldest first).

Use this value when you want earlier sessions to appear before more recent ones in the result set. This setting affects only the presentation order and does not change any underlying data.

Sorting direction for the `created_at` field when ordering admin user sessions in descending chronological order (newest first).

Use this value when you want the most recently created sessions to appear first in the result set. This setting affects only the presentation order and does not change any underlying data.

orderByCreatedAt.description:
Sorting direction to apply when ordering admin user sessions by their `created_at` timestamp.

Accepts either `asc` for ascending order or `desc` for descending order, controlling only how the result set is presented to the caller.

ITodoAppGuestUser.ISummary.description:
Lightweight summary view of a guest user concept in the todoApp service.

This summary type is used wherever the system needs to reference or display guest user information in a compact form, without exposing full internal auditing details.

Guest users represent unauthenticated or anonymous visitors tracked conceptually by the backend. They never own todos directly and are primarily used in authorization, analytics, or future extension points.

The summary exposes both creation and last update timestamps so that administrative tools and analytics pipelines can reason about the lifecycle and recency of each guest concept record without loading the full entity.

id.description:
Unique identifier of the guest user concept record.

This matches the primary key of the `todo_app_guestusers` table and is used to correlate any optional guest metadata across the system.

external_ref.description:
Optional external reference or correlation identifier for this guest concept.

Typical examples include an anonymous analytics ID or a cookie-based tracking token. When null, no persistent external identifier is associated with this guest record.

created_at.description:
Timestamp indicating when this guest concept record was created.

Used for basic auditing, reporting, and retention policies around guest-related data.

updated_at.description:
Timestamp indicating the most recent update to this guest concept record.

This value mirrors the `updated_at` column of the `todo_app_guestusers` table and is useful for understanding when guest-related metadata was last changed and for driving lifecycle or retention heuristics in administrative tooling.

ITodoAppAdminUserSession.ISummary.description:
Summary view of an administrative user's authentication session in the todoApp service.

This DTO is optimized for list views and lightweight embeddings where only high-level session information is required rather than full session detail. It exposes the session identifier, the owning admin user context, basic connection metadata, and key lifecycle timestamps so that administrators can quickly scan and audit active or historical sessions.

The summary intentionally omits any heavy or implementation-specific fields and focuses on values that are stable, safe to expose, and useful for monitoring, troubleshooting, and security review flows.

id.description:
Unique identifier of the admin user session.

This value maps directly to `todo_app_adminuser_sessions.id` and is used to reference or revoke a particular administrative session. It is globally unique across all sessions in the todoApp installation.

adminUser.description:
Summary representation of the administrative user who owns this session.

This reference replaces the raw `todo_app_adminuser_id` foreign key and provides immediate context about which admin account established the session, without requiring additional API calls. It allows list views and audit tools to display key admin attributes (such as name or status) alongside each session row.

ip.description:
IP address from which this administrative session was established.

The value comes from `todo_app_adminuser_sessions.ip` and is recorded at the moment the session is created. It is used for security analytics, anomaly detection, and incident investigation workflows.

href.description:
Full request URL that was accessed when the admin session was created.

This directly reflects `todo_app_adminuser_sessions.href` and captures the concrete entry point into the system at login time. It helps operators understand which admin-facing screen initiated authentication.

referrer.description:
Referrer URL reported by the client when the admin session started.

This maps to `todo_app_adminuser_sessions.referrer` and provides contextual information about how the administrator navigated into the login or protected area, supporting security and UX diagnostics.

created_at.description:
Timestamp when the administrative session was created.

It is the direct projection of `todo_app_adminuser_sessions.created_at` and marks the point at which authentication succeeded and the session became valid.

expired_at.description:
Timestamp when the administrative session expired or was revoked, or null while it remains active.

The value is sourced from `todo_app_adminuser_sessions.expired_at`. A null indicates an active or not-yet-terminated session, whereas a non-null value marks the end of the session's validity window.

A page.

Collection of records with pagination information.

Collection of records with pagination information.

A page.

Collection of records with pagination information.

ITodoAppMemberUserStatus.IUpdate.description:
Update DTO for modifying the business status of a member user account in the todoApp system.

This schema is used exclusively by administrative workflows that need to change the status column of the `todo_app_memberusers` Prisma model while leaving immutable identity fields such as `id` and `email` untouched. Typical status values include `active`, `blocked`, or `disabled`, and they control whether a member is allowed to authenticate and operate on todos.

Implementations should always validate the requested status value against allowed transitions and persist the change in a single transaction that also refreshes the `updated_at` column. This DTO intentionally exposes only the minimal field needed for status management so that administrative clients cannot accidentally modify unrelated profile attributes when calling the status endpoint.

status.description:
New business status value to apply to the member user account.

This string corresponds directly to the `status` column of the `todo_app_memberusers` Prisma model and determines whether the member is considered active, blocked, disabled, or in another well-defined state. Typical implementations constrain this field to a small, predefined set of values such as `active`, `blocked`, and `disabled`.

The backend must validate that the provided status value is recognized and that the transition from the current status to the new status is allowed under configured business rules. Clients should treat this as an opaque but documented enumeration and must not attempt to store user-defined free-form states.

scenario.draft:
Test minimal guest user registration flow via /auth/guestUser/join.

Steps:
1. Call POST /auth/guestUser/join with an empty JSON body (omit external_ref) to represent an anonymous visitor with no external tracking identifier.
2. Verify response status is 201 or other designated success code.
3. Assert that the response body conforms to ITodoAppGuestUser.IAuthorized:
   - Contains a non-empty UUID-formatted id.
   - external_ref is either null or absent, matching DB nullable semantics.
   - created_at and updated_at are valid ISO 8601 date-time strings.
   - token is present and matches IAuthorizationToken shape with access, refresh, expired_at, and refreshable_until fields.
   - Top-level accessToken and refreshToken (if present) mirror token.access and token.refresh values.
4. Confirm that expired_at is not in the past at the time of response, and refreshable_until is greater than or equal to expired_at, reflecting a valid refresh window.
5. Optionally, immediately use the returned access token in a no-op public/guest-safe call if such exists (outside this scenario’s direct scope) to demonstrate that the token is accepted by the auth layer.
6. Ensure that repeated minimal joins yield distinct guest ids and token sets, confirming proper UUID generation and token uniqueness.

Test guest user registration when client supplies an external_ref correlation identifier.

Steps:
1. Prepare a request body matching ITodoAppGuestUser.IJoinRequest with a non-empty, bounded-length external_ref string such as "tracking-abc-123" that represents an opaque analytics or A/B test key.
2. Call POST /auth/guestUser/join with this payload.
3. Verify success status code and response body type ITodoAppGuestUser.IAuthorized.
4. Assert that:
   - The returned id is a UUID and differs across multiple join calls.
   - external_ref in the response equals the supplied value exactly.
   - created_at and updated_at are valid ISO 8601 timestamps; updated_at is greater than or equal to created_at.
   - token.access and token.refresh are non-empty strings; expired_at and refreshable_until are valid future date-times.
   - Top-level accessToken and refreshToken (if present) match token.access and token.refresh.
5. Perform a second join call with a different external_ref value and verify the new guest has a different id and corresponding external_ref, ensuring no cross-contamination between guest concepts.
6. Validate that the service does not echo any additional server-managed fields from todo_app_guestusers beyond those defined in ITodoAppGuestUser.IAuthorized, maintaining DTO contract integrity.

Explore behavior of repeated guest join calls from the same client to understand idempotency expectations and rate-limiting/abuse characteristics (business rule-level check, not infrastructure-level DoS testing).

Steps:
1. Prepare a stable external_ref value such as "client-xyz-device-001".
2. Call POST /auth/guestUser/join multiple times (e.g., 3–5) in quick succession with the same external_ref.
3. For each response, verify ITodoAppGuestUser.IAuthorized structure and that:
   - Each call returns a distinct guest id and token set (i.e., endpoint is not idempotent by external_ref).
   - external_ref returned always equals the provided value.
4. Confirm no validation errors occur solely due to repeated use of identical external_ref, unless specified otherwise by business rules.
5. Optionally measure logical indicators of rate limiting if exposed via headers or error responses (without relying on infrastructure-level details): after a certain number of rapid calls, the service may begin rejecting requests with 4xx errors; if so, assert the error code and basic error body structure.
6. Document expected behavior so that implementers understand whether clients should cache a single guest identity or are allowed to create many guest concepts per device.

Test successful refresh of guestUser authorization tokens using a valid refresh token obtained from a prior join call.

Steps:
1. First, call POST /auth/guestUser/join with a minimal or external_ref payload to obtain an ITodoAppGuestUser.IAuthorized response.
2. Extract the refreshToken (or token.refresh) value from the join response.
3. Build an ITodoAppGuestUser.IRefreshRequest payload containing this refreshToken and, optionally, stable clientId and tokenFamily strings to simulate a concrete client/device.
4. Call POST /auth/guestUser/refresh with this payload.
5. Verify success status code and that response body is ITodoAppGuestUser.IAuthorized.
6. Assert that:
   - The id in the refresh response matches the id from the original join, confirming continuity of the guest concept.
   - external_ref, created_at, and updated_at are present and logically consistent (updated_at may be equal to or later than the original value, depending on implementation).
   - New token.access and token.refresh differ from the previous pair, demonstrating token rotation.
   - New expired_at and refreshable_until extend or at least re-establish a valid authentication and refresh window.
   - Top-level accessToken and refreshToken mirror the nested token values.
7. Optionally perform a second refresh using the newest refresh token to ensure chained refresh is allowed within refreshable_until constraints.

dependencies.purpose: Obtain an initial ITodoAppGuestUser.IAuthorized payload and valid refresh token for the guestUser actor.

scenario.draft:
Validate that the refresh endpoint correctly accepts and processes optional clientId and tokenFamily metadata without breaking token issuance.

Steps:
1. Call POST /auth/guestUser/join to obtain an authorized guest response and extract the refresh token.
2. Construct an ITodoAppGuestUser.IRefreshRequest payload including:
   - refreshToken: value from the join response.
   - clientId: a realistic identifier for a client application or device, e.g., "web-spa-1".
   - tokenFamily: a string such as "fam-guest-001" representing a refresh token family.
3. Invoke POST /auth/guestUser/refresh with this payload.
4. Verify that the response is successful and of type ITodoAppGuestUser.IAuthorized.
5. Assert that the returned id matches the original guest id.
6. Confirm that the presence of clientId and tokenFamily does not change the DTO shape: token, accessToken, refreshToken, and timestamps are all present and valid.
7. Optionally perform another refresh using the newly issued refresh token and the same clientId/tokenFamily to validate continuous token family handling at a behavioral level (without inspecting server-internal state).

dependencies.purpose: Create an initial guestUser concept and obtain a refresh token to use with clientId/tokenFamily metadata.

scenario.draft:
Test negative refresh behavior when providing invalid or improperly reused refresh tokens for a guestUser.

Steps:
1. Call POST /auth/guestUser/join to obtain a valid refresh token.
2. Construct three variants of ITodoAppGuestUser.IRefreshRequest payloads:
   - Variant A: A clearly malformed refreshToken string, such as "not-a-jwt".
   - Variant B: A structurally valid-looking token that is not issued by the system (if available from fixtures), or a randomly generated long string.
   - Variant C: Optionally, after a successful refresh, attempt to reuse the old refresh token in a second refresh request to simulate replay (if the implementation enforces one-time use per token).
3. For each variant, call POST /auth/guestUser/refresh and verify that:
   - The API returns an appropriate 401/403-style error for invalid or unauthorized tokens.
   - The error body follows the service’s standard error response shape (status code, error message, etc.) without leaking sensitive validation details.
4. Confirm that no ITodoAppGuestUser.IAuthorized payload is returned in failure cases and that no new tokens are issued for invalid or replayed tokens.
5. Optionally, after failing refresh attempts, use the original access token from the join response (if not yet expired) against a protected endpoint (if available elsewhere) to determine whether failed refresh attempts affect existing access tokens, and document the observed behavior for client guidance.

dependencies.purpose: Issue an initial valid refresh token to use as baseline for invalid/reuse scenarios.

scenario.draft:
Verify that registration accepts and persists an optional displayName field.

Workflow:
1. Prepare a join payload with a unique email, strong password, and a non-empty displayName along with required href/referrer and optional ip.
2. Call POST /auth/memberUser/join.
3. Confirm success status and that the response ITodoAppMemberUser.IAuthorized contains:
   - display_name equal to the sent displayName string.
   - Other identity and token fields correctly populated.
4. Optionally, in a later test using admin/member inspection APIs, confirm that the stored profile for this user also returns the same display name (if such endpoints exist in other plan groups).

Business rules validated:
- displayName is correctly accepted and not ignored.
- display_name in the authorized payload is synchronized with the stored profile.

Ensure that registering with an email that already exists in todo_app_memberusers is rejected and does not create a second account.

Workflow:
1. First, register a member user via POST /auth/memberUser/join with a specific email, password, and href/referrer; assert success and note the email.
2. Attempt a second POST /auth/memberUser/join using the same email but a different password and possibly different displayName.
3. Assert that the second request fails with an appropriate error status (e.g., 409 Conflict or 400 depending on contract) and that the response body indicates an email uniqueness or duplicate-account problem (message/code, without leaking password details).
4. Optionally, validate via any available listing or lookup API in other test plan groups that there is still only one user with that email.

Business rules validated:
- Unique constraint on todo_app_memberusers.email is enforced at the API level.
- Duplicate registration attempts do not create additional accounts.
- Error responses distinguish conflict from generic server errors.

Confirm that the join endpoint never returns or exposes the raw password or password_hash fields.

Workflow:
1. Send a normal registration request to POST /auth/memberUser/join including a clearly recognizable password string.
2. On successful response, perform a strict inspection of the ITodoAppMemberUser.IAuthorized payload:
   - Verify that there is no field named password, password_hash, or other sensitive credential-like fields.
   - Confirm that the only credential data returned are the JWT access and refresh tokens inside token, which are opaque.
3. Optionally, if logs are accessible in the test harness, ensure that the password value is not logged as part of request/response snapshots beyond what the test framework securely stores.

Business rules validated:
- Credential secrecy is maintained at the API boundary.
- The system relies on password_hash stored server-side, but that detail is never surfaced to clients.

Validate that the join endpoint accepts and uses connection metadata (ip, href, referrer) to initialize session context.

Workflow:
1. Construct a join payload with realistic ip, href, and referrer values (ensuring href and referrer satisfy URI format and required presence). Use a unique email and password.
2. Call POST /auth/memberUser/join and assert success.
3. Although the join response does not expose raw session records, design follow-up tests (in other plan groups) that retrieve session details via member or admin session listing APIs to confirm that the new session row reflects the supplied ip, href, and referrer.

Business rules validated:
- Session-related metadata is accepted on registration and can later be audited.
- The DTO fields for ip, href, and referrer are wired through to session creation logic.

Validate that a member user who has just registered can log in using the same credentials and receive a fresh authorized payload.

Workflow:
1. Register a new member via POST /auth/memberUser/join with a unique email and password plus required href/referrer, capturing the chosen email and password.
2. Call POST /auth/memberUser/login with ITodoAppMemberUserLogin.ICreate using the same email and password and realistic href/referrer (and optional ip).
3. Assert that login succeeds with an ITodoAppMemberUser.IAuthorized response containing:
   - id, email, display_name, status, created_at, updated_at.
   - token fields (access, refresh, expired_at, refreshable_until) all present and valid.
4. Optionally, compare login response identity fields to those from join to ensure consistent id and email, and compatible status.
5. Optionally, use the access token from login to call a member-protected endpoint in a later test to confirm token usability.

Business rules validated:
- Newly registered accounts can authenticate immediately.
- Login uses email/password exactly as stored during join.
- A new authorized context (tokens) is correctly issued on login.

dependencies.purpose: Create a member user account so that valid credentials exist for login testing.

scenario.draft:
Ensure that login fails when the correct email is provided with an incorrect password and no tokens are issued.

Workflow:
1. Register a member via POST /auth/memberUser/join, capturing the email and correct password.
2. Construct a login payload to POST /auth/memberUser/login using the same email but a deliberately incorrect password value, and valid href/referrer.
3. Assert that the login attempt fails with an authentication error status (e.g., 401 Unauthorized) and that the response body does not reveal whether the email exists (generic invalid credentials message).
4. Confirm that the response does not contain an ITodoAppMemberUser.IAuthorized structure or any JWT tokens.

Business rules validated:
- Password verification is enforced; mismatched passwords are rejected.
- Error handling does not leak account existence details.
- No tokens are granted when authentication fails.

dependencies.purpose: Provision a valid member account to ensure that only the password causes login failure.

scenario.draft:
Check that login attempts with an email not present in todo_app_memberusers are rejected without revealing whether the email exists.

Workflow:
1. Optionally register a different member via POST /auth/memberUser/join to ensure the system is operational.
2. Call POST /auth/memberUser/login with a syntactically valid but non-registered email and any password, plus required href/referrer.
3. Assert that the API returns an authentication failure status and a generic invalid-credentials style error.
4. Confirm that no ITodoAppMemberUser.IAuthorized payload or tokens are returned.

Business rules validated:
- Nonexistent accounts cannot be logged into.
- The login endpoint does not distinguish between unknown-email and wrong-password in its external behavior, preserving security posture.

dependencies.purpose: Use a successful join as a sanity check for the environment before attempting login with a different, unknown email.

scenario.draft:
Validate that member account status stored in todo_app_memberusers influences login eligibility (e.g., blocked/disabled users cannot log in).

Workflow:
1. Register a member via POST /auth/memberUser/join and capture the resulting member id and email. This yields an initial active status.
2. Using administrative or member-management endpoints from other test plan groups (e.g., an admin-only status update API), change the user’s status to a non-login-allowed state such as blocked or disabled.
3. Attempt to log in with POST /auth/memberUser/login using the same email and correct password, plus required href/referrer.
4. Assert that the login is rejected with an appropriate status (e.g., 403 Forbidden or 401 Unauthorized) and that no tokens are issued.

Business rules validated:
- Business status field in todo_app_memberusers controls authentication eligibility.
- Status transitions outside this endpoint are honored by the login logic.

dependencies.purpose: Create a baseline active member account before status modification via admin/member management APIs.

scenario.draft:
Verify that each successful login call records a new session in todo_app_memberuser_sessions, using the provided connection metadata.

Workflow:
1. Register a member via POST /auth/memberUser/join with connection context (ip, href, referrer) and capture the email/password.
2. Call POST /auth/memberUser/login with the same credentials and another set of ip, href, and referrer values.
3. Assert that login returns a valid ITodoAppMemberUser.IAuthorized payload with tokens.
4. In follow-up tests using dedicated session listing APIs (e.g., member or admin session queries in other plan groups), verify that a new session row was created for this login and that it contains the expected ip, href, referrer, created_at, and null expired_at fields.

Business rules validated:
- Each successful login generates a persistent session record.
- Connection metadata from ITodoAppMemberUserLogin.ICreate is properly recorded for auditability.

dependencies.purpose: Create a member account whose sessions will later be audited after login.

scenario.draft:
Test successful admin login with valid credentials and full context metadata.

Steps:
1. Prepare a pre-existing admin user record in todo_app_adminusers with status set to an allowed value (e.g., active) and a known email/password_hash pair.
2. Call POST /auth/adminUser/login with ITodoAppAdminUser.ILogin payload using the correct email and matching plaintext password, along with realistic href and referrer URIs and an optional ip.
3. Assert that the response status indicates success (e.g., 201/200) and the body conforms to ITodoAppAdminUser.IAuthorized.
4. Verify that the token field is present and matches IAuthorizationToken structure, including non-empty access and refresh tokens and valid ISO 8601 timestamps for expired_at and refreshable_until.
5. Confirm that id, email, display_name, status, created_at, and updated_at fields match the underlying admin record (except for any intentionally nullable display_name) and that status still represents an allowed value.
6. Optionally verify that a new row has been inserted into todo_app_adminuser_sessions with todo_app_adminuser_id pointing to the admin’s id and that ip, href, referrer, created_at, and expired_at (null at creation) are persisted as expected.
7. Check that the issued access token can subsequently be used to call an admin-protected endpoint in a separate test to confirm end-to-end authorization wiring.

Test admin login failure when the password is incorrect while the email exists.

Steps:
1. Prepare a pre-existing admin user in todo_app_adminusers with a known email and password_hash and with status set to an allowed state such as active.
2. Call POST /auth/adminUser/login with ITodoAppAdminUser.ILogin payload using the correct email but an incorrect plaintext password; include valid-looking href and referrer values and optional ip.
3. Assert that the response status indicates authentication failure (e.g., 401/403) and that no ITodoAppAdminUser.IAuthorized payload is returned.
4. Verify that the error message does not reveal whether the email or password was incorrect, preserving security best practices.
5. Ensure that no new todo_app_adminuser_sessions entry is created for this attempt, or that any side-channel logging does not mark the session as valid.
6. Optionally repeat with multiple incorrect attempts to verify that the behavior remains consistent and that no partial session artifacts leak through.

Test admin login failure when the email address is not registered.

Steps:
1. Ensure that no admin record exists in todo_app_adminusers with the test email (e.g., by choosing a clearly synthetic domain or cleaning up any prior records if needed).
2. Call POST /auth/adminUser/login with ITodoAppAdminUser.ILogin payload using a non-existent email, an arbitrary password, and valid href/referrer values.
3. Assert that the response status indicates authentication failure (e.g., 401/403) and that the error message is generic and does not reveal that the email is unregistered.
4. Confirm that the response body does not match ITodoAppAdminUser.IAuthorized, and that no token field is present or usable.
5. Verify that no new row is written to todo_app_adminuser_sessions for this attempt.
6. Optionally confirm that rate limiting or logging can be integrated with repeated attempts without changing the outward error semantics.

Test that admin login is blocked when the admin’s status in todo_app_adminusers represents a non-operational state.

Steps:
1. Prepare a todo_app_adminusers record with the test email and password_hash, but set status to a value representing a blocked or suspended condition (e.g., suspended or disabled) according to business rules.
2. Call POST /auth/adminUser/login with ITodoAppAdminUser.ILogin payload using the correct email and matching password, and include valid href/referrer values.
3. Assert that the response status indicates authentication failure, not success, and that no ITodoAppAdminUser.IAuthorized body or tokens are returned.
4. Verify that the error message remains generic and does not explicitly state that the account is suspended.
5. Confirm that either no new todo_app_adminuser_sessions row is created, or that any internal representation of the attempt is clearly marked as invalid and cannot be used to mint tokens.
6. Optionally flip the status back to an allowed state and repeat the login to confirm that the same credentials now succeed, demonstrating that login behavior is gated by the status column.

Test that admin login enforces required context fields and persists them to the session record correctly.

Steps:
1. Prepare a valid admin record in todo_app_adminusers with active status and known email/password_hash.
2. Call POST /auth/adminUser/login with ITodoAppAdminUser.ILogin payload omitting ip but supplying valid href and referrer values that satisfy URI formatting and business expectations.
3. Assert that the login succeeds and that the response conforms to ITodoAppAdminUser.IAuthorized.
4. Inspect the created todo_app_adminuser_sessions record and verify that ip is either set to the provided value or, if omitted, derived from the connection, while href and referrer exactly match the submitted values.
5. Attempt to call the endpoint with missing or malformed href or referrer to confirm that such requests are rejected or validated according to the schema and business rules, while not testing low-level framework validation messages.
6. Optionally confirm that repeated logins from different href/referrer combinations create distinct session rows capturing their own context metadata.

Test successful rotation of admin JWT tokens using a valid refresh token.

Steps:
1. Ensure that there is an existing valid session row in todo_app_adminuser_sessions linked to an active admin in todo_app_adminusers (this may be prepared via a setup script or a prior login call in a separate test).
2. Obtain a valid refresh token associated with that session, consistent with ITodoAppAdminUser.IRefresh.refresh_token semantics.
3. Call POST /auth/adminUser/refresh with ITodoAppAdminUser.IRefresh payload containing the valid refresh_token.
4. Assert that the response status indicates success and that the body conforms to ITodoAppAdminUser.IAuthorized.
5. Verify that the returned id, email, display_name, status, created_at, and updated_at correspond to the owning admin user and that status remains in an allowed state.
6. Confirm that the token field is present and that the new access and refresh values differ from the previous ones, with updated expired_at and refreshable_until timestamps consistent with rotation policies.
7. Optionally check that the underlying todo_app_adminuser_sessions record is still considered valid (e.g., expired_at remains null or in the future) and that any updated expiration behavior is applied consistently.

Test that token refresh fails when the referenced admin session is expired, revoked, or otherwise invalid.

Steps:
1. Prepare a todo_app_adminuser_sessions row for a known admin such that its expired_at is set in the past or that it is otherwise marked as no longer valid for refresh according to business rules.
2. Generate or capture a refresh token that would normally map to this now-invalid session.
3. Call POST /auth/adminUser/refresh with ITodoAppAdminUser.IRefresh payload containing that refresh_token.
4. Assert that the response status indicates failure (e.g., 401/403) and that no ITodoAppAdminUser.IAuthorized payload is returned.
5. Verify that the error message is generic and does not reveal whether the session, the token signature, or the underlying admin record caused the failure.
6. Confirm that no new valid tokens are issued and that the invalid session cannot be refreshed again.
7. Optionally attempt to refresh multiple times to ensure consistent behavior and absence of partial reactivation side effects.

Test that token refresh is denied when the admin account’s status has changed to a blocked state since session creation.

Steps:
1. Create an admin user in todo_app_adminusers with an initially allowed status and establish a valid session plus refresh_token through prior login.
2. Update the admin’s status in todo_app_adminusers to a restricted state (e.g., suspended or disabled) after the session has been established but before attempting refresh.
3. Call POST /auth/adminUser/refresh with ITodoAppAdminUser.IRefresh payload containing the original refresh_token.
4. Assert that the response indicates authentication/authorization failure and that no new tokens are issued.
5. Verify that the error message does not leak detailed status information, while business logs can reflect the status-based denial.
6. Confirm that the still-time-valid session in todo_app_adminuser_sessions is effectively neutralized for refresh because the owning admin’s status is no longer acceptable.
7. Optionally revert the status to an allowed state and repeat to confirm that refresh then succeeds, demonstrating that refresh behavior is driven by current admin status, not just session timestamps.

Test that refresh rejects structurally invalid or tampered refresh tokens.

Steps:
1. Prepare the system with at least one valid admin session and refresh token, but for this test construct an obviously malformed refresh_token string (e.g., truncated, not base64, or random noise) that cannot map to any todo_app_adminuser_sessions row.
2. Call POST /auth/adminUser/refresh with ITodoAppAdminUser.IRefresh payload using the malformed refresh_token value.
3. Assert that the response status indicates failure and that no ITodoAppAdminUser.IAuthorized payload or tokens are returned.
4. Verify that the error response is generic and does not expose internal validation details, such as signature verification errors or token parsing internals.
5. Ensure that no new session entry is created and nothing about existing sessions is modified as a side effect of the failed refresh.
6. Optionally try a token that is structurally valid but signed for a different actor or session to confirm that cross-actor or cross-session tokens are also rejected without leaking additional information.

Test that refresh produces new tokens while preserving admin identity and audit characteristics.

Steps:
1. Start with a known admin account and a valid session plus associated refresh_token from a prior successful login.
2. Record the current ITodoAppAdminUser.IAuthorized representation and token values from that login, especially id, email, display_name, status, and created_at/updated_at.
3. Call POST /auth/adminUser/refresh with ITodoAppAdminUser.IRefresh payload containing the valid refresh_token.
4. Assert that the response is successful and returns ITodoAppAdminUser.IAuthorized.
5. Verify that id, email, display_name, status, created_at, and updated_at fields are unchanged relative to the original authorized view of the admin, confirming that identity and account metadata are preserved.
6. Confirm that the token.access and token.refresh values differ from the previous ones and that expired_at and refreshable_until timestamps are moved forward according to policy.
7. Optionally check that the actor encoded in the new tokens still maps to the same admin id and that any subsequent admin-only endpoint calls using the new access token succeed, proving end-to-end continuity of permissions after rotation.

Validate that an authenticated admin user can retrieve detailed information for a specific member user who already has at least one todo and that all key profile and lifecycle fields are correctly populated.

Workflow:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to register and authenticate a new admin user, obtaining an access token representing an administrative actor.
2. Call POST /todoApp/adminUser/systemSettings as that admin to create a baseline system setting (for example, a feature flag or limit) so that admin tooling and configuration-dependent logic are initialized.
3. Using a separate member authentication flow (assumed handled by the system), create at least one todo for a member user via POST /todoApp/memberUser/todos, ensuring the todo is owned by the target memberUserId that will be inspected.
4. As the authenticated admin, call GET /todoApp/adminUser/memberUsers/{memberUserId} with the target memberUserId corresponding to the member who owns the created todo.
5. Assert that the response status is 200 and that the body matches ITodoAppMemberUser: it contains the correct id, email, optional display_name, status, and created_at/updated_at timestamps.
6. Verify that the returned memberUser reflects the expected business status (for example, active) and that identity fields (id and email) match the member that owns the created todo.
7. Optionally verify that timestamps are consistent with the order of operations (created_at before updated_at and both before the time of retrieval).

scenario.draft:
Test listing current member user's sessions with default pagination and no filters.

1. Use POST /auth/memberUser/join to register a new member user and obtain initial authorized tokens.
2. Use the returned access token to perform several authenticated actions that implicitly create or reuse at least one member session according to implementation (or rely on the initial session from join/login).
3. Call PATCH /todoApp/memberUser/actors/current/sessions with an ITodoAppSession.IRequest body that only sets required pagination fields (e.g., page=0, limit=20) and leaves all optional filters (ip, createdFrom/To, expiredFrom/To, activeOnly) null or omitted.
4. Assert that the response status is 200 and the body conforms to IPageITodoAppSession.ISummary:
   - pagination.current equals the requested page (0).
   - pagination.limit equals the requested limit.
   - pagination.records is >= 1 and pagination.pages is >= 1.
   - data is an array with at least one ITodoAppSession.ISummary element.
5. For at least one element in data, verify that:
   - id is a non-empty UUID string.
   - actor_type is "member" (since we authenticated as memberUser).
   - actor_id matches the authenticated member's id.
   - ip, href, referrer are non-empty strings consistent with the test client setup.
   - created_at is a valid ISO date-time.
6. Ensure that no sessions belonging to any other actor are present and that the API does not leak admin sessions or other users’ sessions.

scenario.draft:
Test filtering current member user's sessions by creation time window.

1. Register a new member user via POST /auth/memberUser/join and capture tokens and actor id.
2. Immediately perform an authenticated request that ensures a session exists and note the approximate current time T0 from the test runner.
3. Build an ITodoAppSession.IRequest body for PATCH /todoApp/memberUser/actors/current/sessions:
   - page=0, limit=10
   - createdFrom set to (T0 minus a small buffer, e.g., 1 minute) as ISO 8601 date-time.
   - createdTo set to (T0 plus a small buffer, e.g., 1 minute).
   - All other filters (ip, expiredFrom, expiredTo, activeOnly) null or omitted.
4. Call PATCH /todoApp/memberUser/actors/current/sessions with this body using the member's access token.
5. Assert that the response includes at least the current active session and that for each returned ITodoAppSession.ISummary, created_at lies within [createdFrom, createdTo].
6. Optionally perform a second call with a non-overlapping time window (e.g., both createdFrom and createdTo several hours in the past) and verify that the result set is empty or excludes the current session, confirming that the date filters are effective.
7. Validate pagination information and ensure no sessions for other actors are included.

scenario.draft:
Test pagination behavior when the member user has more sessions than fit in a single page.

1. Register a member user with POST /auth/memberUser/join.
2. Using the same credentials or flows that create sessions (e.g., repeated login flows if available, or repeated context that causes new session creation), generate more than N sessions, where N is a small page size such as 5.
3. Call PATCH /todoApp/memberUser/actors/current/sessions with ITodoAppSession.IRequest:
   - page=0
   - limit=5
   - all filters null or omitted.
4. Assert 200 response and that:
   - pagination.limit is 5
   - pagination.current is 0
   - pagination.records is greater than 5
   - pagination.pages is greater than 1
   - data length is <= 5.
5. Call the same endpoint again with:
   - page=1
   - limit=5.
6. Assert that the second page returns a different subset of sessions (no duplicate id set compared to page 0 within the same call set) and that ITodoAppSession.ISummary.id values across pages are unique within the union of results seen so far.
7. Confirm consistent actor_type and actor_id for all sessions and that pagination metadata matches the union of all pages.

scenario.draft:
Test terminating a single active session belonging to the current member user.

1. Register a new member user via POST /auth/memberUser/join to create an initial session and obtain tokens.
2. Call PATCH /todoApp/memberUser/actors/current/sessions with page=0, limit=10 and activeOnly=true to discover the active sessions for this user. Extract the id of one active session (sessionIdTarget).
3. Using the same authenticated context, call DELETE /todoApp/memberUser/actors/current/sessions/{sessionIdTarget} with the sessionId path parameter set to the selected id.
4. Assert that the response status code indicates successful termination (e.g., 200 or 204 depending on implementation) and that no response body is returned when none is defined.
5. Call PATCH /todoApp/memberUser/actors/current/sessions again with activeOnly=true and page=0, limit=10.
6. Verify that the terminated session no longer appears in the active list and, if the implementation keeps historical records, that its expired_at is now non-null when listed without the activeOnly filter.
7. Ensure that no other sessions owned by this user are inadvertently removed or altered aside from the one targeted for termination.

scenario.draft:
Test a workflow where the user iteratively terminates all sessions except the current one, simulating "log out from other devices" behavior using the session listing and termination endpoints.

1. Register a new member user via POST /auth/memberUser/join.
2. Using that account, create multiple sessions (e.g., by performing separate login flows in different logical clients if supported, or repeated token-issuing flows) so that the user has several active sessions.
3. From a chosen "primary" client with a known access token, call PATCH /todoApp/memberUser/actors/current/sessions with activeOnly=true, page=0, limit set large enough to retrieve all active sessions.
4. Identify the current session for the primary client by comparing connection metadata (e.g., ip, href, referrer) or by a known sessionId stored in that client; mark this as sessionIdCurrent.
5. For each other session summary returned (those whose id != sessionIdCurrent), invoke DELETE /todoApp/memberUser/actors/current/sessions/{sessionId} using the primary client's token.
6. After iterating through all non-current sessions, call the PATCH listing endpoint again with activeOnly=true.
7. Assert that only the current session remains active in the returned data and that all previously terminated sessions are either missing from the active list or visible only as historical (expired_at not null) when activeOnly is false.
8. Confirm that the primary client's own token/session remains valid and usable for performing subsequent protected operations, proving that self-termination was avoided.

scenario.draft:
Test idempotent or safe behavior when attempting to terminate a session that has already been terminated for the current member user.

1. Register a new member user via POST /auth/memberUser/join.

4. Immediately call DELETE /todoApp/memberUser/actors/current/sessions/{sessionIdTarget} again with the same authenticated context.
5. Assert that the system responds in a safe and predictable way:
   - Either returns a not-found or similar error without exposing whether the session ever existed for another actor, or
   - Returns a success/no-op status indicating idempotent termination, but does not resurrect or recreate the session.
6. If the system returns an error response, validate that the error format matches global error-handling conventions (status codes, error body shape) defined for the service and does not leak sensitive information.
7. Optionally call the listing endpoint again to confirm the session remains non-active and that no duplicate or phantom sessions were created as a result of repeated deletes.

scenario.draft:
Validate that an authenticated admin can erase a specific member user session after the member has actively used the system.

Flow:
1. Initialize system configuration by creating a global system setting so that member-related features and limits are defined.
2. Create an admin account via join and obtain admin authorization tokens.
3. Using the admin tokens, create at least one global system setting record if not already created (idempotent from the test perspective) to ensure configuration consistency.
4. Register a new member user via the dedicated member join/auth flow (assumed available in the broader API set) and obtain tokens for that member.
5. As the member user, create at least one todo using POST /todoApp/memberUser/todos so that a valid member user exists with associated activity in todo_app_todos and an authentication session.
6. As the admin user (using admin tokens), search the member users and/or their sessions (using the broader admin/member APIs) to discover the concrete memberUserId and sessionId that correspond to the member’s active session.
7. Call DELETE /todoApp/adminUser/memberUsers/{memberUserId}/sessions/{sessionId} with the admin’s Authorization header targeting the discovered memberUserId and sessionId.
8. Assert that the response indicates successful deletion (e.g., appropriate 2xx status and empty or minimal body).
9. Optionally, attempt to use the erased session token as the member user in a subsequent call (e.g., a member todo operation) and verify that authentication fails due to the revoked session, confirming the session record is effectively invalidated.

scenario.draft:
Validate that an authenticated admin can search administrative users with combined email and status filters and receive a correctly paginated list.

Flow:
1. Initialize global configuration by creating at least one system setting via POST /todoApp/adminUser/systemSettings to reflect a realistic administrative environment.
2. Register an initial admin account via /auth/adminUser/join and obtain admin tokens to authorize subsequent admin operations.
3. (Optionally via broader API set) Ensure there are multiple admin users in the system with varying emails and statuses so that filtering has observable impact.
4. As the authenticated admin, call PATCH /todoApp/adminUser/adminUsers with an ITodoAppAdminUser.IRequest payload that specifies:
   - page and limit values (e.g., page 1, limit 10),
   - an email filter substring or exact email,
   - a specific status such as "active",
   - and optionally an orderByCreatedAt direction.
5. Verify that the response body is an IPageITodoAppAdminUser.ISummary structure, where:
   - pagination.current and pagination.limit reflect the requested page and limit,
   - pagination.records and pagination.pages are consistent with the total number of matching admin users,
   - each entry in data is an ITodoAppAdminUser.ISummary whose email and status satisfy the filters.
6. Confirm that admin users not matching the email or status filters do not appear in the data list, and that sorting by created_at follows the requested order direction.

8. Confirm that pagination.records remains constant across both calls and accurately reflects the total number of adminUser records.

scenario.draft:
Verify that an authenticated adminUser can successfully and irreversibly delete another administrative user once required system settings and policies exist.

Steps:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to register Admin A (the acting administrator) and obtain its authorization tokens.
2. Using Admin A’s token, call POST /todoApp/adminUser/systemSettings to create at least one configuration entry that represents administrative environment/policies required before destructive operations (for example, a flag that enables admin deletion or defines retention behavior).
3. Still as Admin A, call POST /auth/adminUser/join again to create Admin B, the target account to be deleted. Capture Admin B’s id from the ITodoAppAdminUser.IAuthorized payload.
4. Call DELETE /todoApp/adminUser/adminUsers/{adminUserId} as Admin A, passing Admin B’s id in the path.
5. Assert that the DELETE request returns the expected success status code (e.g., 204 or 200) with no response body.
6. Attempt to retrieve Admin B via a suitable adminUsers GET or search endpoint (if available in the broader API) or via a subsequent management call; verify that Admin B no longer exists or is otherwise not returned.
7. Confirm that Admin A remains unaffected and can continue using admin endpoints.

Business rules validated:
- Destructive delete of an admin user is only allowed for authenticated adminUser actors.
- Required system settings must exist before performing irreversible admin deletion.
- Deleting one admin does not cascade to other admins or system settings.

scenario.draft:
Validate business rules around an admin attempting to delete their own administrative account, ensuring that either it is allowed with proper effects or explicitly prohibited according to policy, while required system settings exist.

Steps:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to create and authenticate Admin A (the only admin used in this scenario).
2. As Admin A, call POST /todoApp/adminUser/systemSettings to create a configuration entry that defines or reflects policies around self-deletion (for example, a flag that controls whether an admin can delete their own account).
3. Still as Admin A, call DELETE /todoApp/adminUser/adminUsers/{adminUserId} with adminUserId set to Admin A’s own id from the join response.
4. Observe the response:
   - If self-deletion is allowed, expect a success status code and verify that subsequent admin-authenticated operations fail because the account no longer exists.
   - If self-deletion is disallowed, expect a domain-specific error status (e.g., 400 or 403) and verify that Admin A’s account remains present by attempting another authenticated admin operation that should still succeed.

Business rules validated:
- System honors policy defined in system settings regarding whether an admin can delete themselves.
- Self-deletion behavior is consistent: either account is fully removed and subsequent admin usage fails, or the deletion is blocked and the account remains operational.
- Required system settings are established before testing the self-deletion rule.

Steps:
1. Call POST /todoApp/adminUser/systemSettings without any Authorization header, attempting to create system settings anonymously. Expect this to fail with an authorization error because only adminUser actors should manage system settings.
2. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to create and authenticate Admin A.
3. As Admin A, call POST /todoApp/adminUser/systemSettings to successfully create required system settings.
4. As Admin A, call POST /auth/adminUser/join again to create Admin B, the target admin account for deletion; capture Admin B’s id.
5. Attempt to call DELETE /todoApp/adminUser/adminUsers/{adminUserId} with Admin B’s id but intentionally omit the Authorization header or provide an invalid token.
6. Verify that the delete request fails with an authentication/authorization error (for example, 401 or 403) and that Admin B still exists by performing an authorized admin GET/search in later tests.

Business rules validated:
- SystemSettings and admin deletion endpoints both require authenticated adminUser context.
- Irreversible deletion cannot be executed by anonymous or improperly authenticated clients, even if system settings are configured.
- Authentication is consistently enforced for destructive admin operations.

scenario.draft:
Verify that an authenticated adminUser can change another admin’s status to a suspended-like state, with system settings defining allowed transitions, and that this status blocks further logins for that admin.

Steps:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to create and authenticate Admin A (policy-controlling admin).
2. As Admin A, call POST /todoApp/adminUser/systemSettings to create at least one configuration entry that describes or enables status transition rules (for example, allowed states: active, suspended, disabled).
3. Still as Admin A, call POST /auth/adminUser/join again to create Admin B, initially active; capture Admin B’s id.
4. As Admin A, call PUT /todoApp/adminUser/adminUsers/{adminUserId}/status with adminUserId set to Admin B’s id and request body ITodoAppAdminUser.IUpdateStatus.status set to a suspended-like value (e.g., "suspended"), and optionally provide a reason.
5. Assert that the response returns HTTP 200 with a full ITodoAppAdminUser body reflecting the new status and updated updated_at timestamp.
6. Attempt to log in as Admin B using POST /auth/adminUser/login with Admin B’s credentials; verify that the login is rejected due to the non-active status.

Business rules validated:
- Only authenticated adminUser actors can change other admins’ statuses.
- Status transitions respect policies defined via system settings.
- Suspended status effectively prevents further authentication for the affected admin account.

Steps:

   - limit: 5

Business rules:
- Admin search must support combining status filters, free-text search, and created_at range filters.
- Sorting must be deterministic and follow order_by and order_direction rules so that administrative UIs can rely on stable ordering.

- Verify that the targeted session is correctly linked to the specified adminUserId and that a valid, linked session can be deleted.

scenario.draft:
Ensure that PATCH /todoApp/adminUser/systemSettings correctly handles pagination across multiple pages for an admin, including boundary pages with partial data and empty results beyond the last page.

Workflow:
1. Join an admin via /auth/adminUser/join and capture its token.
2. Create more system settings via POST /todoApp/adminUser/systemSettings than a chosen pageSize (e.g., create 25 settings, pageSize=10) to require at least three pages.
3. Request page 1 via PATCH /todoApp/adminUser/systemSettings with ITodoAppSystemSetting.IRequest specifying page=1 and pageSize=10, with no additional filters.
4. Assert 200 OK and verify that:
   - pagination.current=1,
   - pagination.limit=10,
   - pagination.records is >= 25,
   - pagination.pages is at least 3,
   - data length is 10.
5. Request page 2 with the same pageSize and verify equivalent checks while ensuring that the returned ITodoAppSystemSetting.ISummary items are distinct from page 1 (no duplicates between pages for a stable sort).
6. Request the last page (pagination.pages from prior responses) and verify that data length is <= pageSize and that records on that page are distinct from earlier pages.
7. Request a page beyond the last (e.g., page=pages+1) and verify that the endpoint returns an empty data array with correct pagination metadata (current reflects requested page, records and pages unchanged).

scenario.draft:

2. Using the admin token, call POST /todoApp/adminUser/systemSettings with a unique key (e.g., "max_active_todos_per_user"), value, type, description, group, and enabled=true to create an active system setting.
3. Still as the same admin, call DELETE /todoApp/adminUser/systemSettings/{settingKey} with the previously created key.

5. Call GET /todoApp/adminUser/systemSettings/{settingKey} as the same admin and assert that the API behaves as if the setting no longer exists (e.g., 404 or equivalent not-found), confirming that deleted settings are not retrievable as active configuration.
6. Optionally, list system settings via PATCH /todoApp/adminUser/systemSettings and verify that the deleted setting is not present in active results, or is only visible through specific filters if supported.
7. Throughout, confirm that only an authenticated admin can perform the delete, and that no unauthenticated call is accepted.

Business rules to validate:
- Deleting a setting uses the business key, not the internal UUID.
- The delete operation performs a soft delete (deleted_at set, enabled typically false) rather than physical row removal.
- Only adminUser actors may delete system settings; public or member users must be rejected.
- Attempting to delete a non-existent or already-deleted key should result in a not-found style error, not a silent success.

scenario.draft:
Validate that a member user can reopen their own todo that was previously marked as completed, restoring it to an active state and making it visible again in normal todo listings.

Scenario outline:
1. Call POST /auth/memberUser/join to register a new member user and obtain authorization tokens for that user.
2. As the same authenticated member, ensure any required system settings exist by calling POST /todoApp/adminUser/systemSettings beforehand via an admin context (see dependencies for setup) so that todo creation rules such as max_active_todos_per_user are satisfied.
3. Using the member user access token, call POST /todoApp/memberUser/todos with a valid ITodoAppTodo.ICreate payload where state is initially set to an allowed active/pending value and, optionally, due_date is in the future. Capture the returned todoId.
4. Still as the same member, call PUT /todoApp/memberUser/todos/{todoId}/complete (from available operations) to mark the todo as completed and verify in the response that state reflects a completed status and completed_at is non-null.
5. Call PUT /todoApp/memberUser/todos/{todoId}/reopen for that todoId, authenticated as the same member user.
6. Assert that the response status is success, that the returned ITodoAppTodo indicates state has transitioned back to an active/pending value, completed_at is null or updated according to lifecycle rules, deleted_at remains null, and updated_at is later than before.
7. Optionally, verify via GET /todoApp/memberUser/todos/{todoId} or a search endpoint that the todo now appears in active lists and that no duplicate records were created.

Key business validations:
- Only the owner member user can reopen their own todo.
- A completed todo can transition back to an active state using the reopen endpoint.
- Lifecycle timestamps (completed_at, updated_at, deleted_at) are consistent with the reopen action.
- System settings that constrain todo behavior do not block a valid reopen of an existing todo.

scenario.draft:
Verify that a member user can restore a logically deleted todo by reopening it, ensuring that deleted_at is cleared and the todo becomes visible again, assuming business rules permit reopening from soft-deleted state.

Scenario outline:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join to create an admin user and POST /todoApp/adminUser/systemSettings if necessary to configure behavior related to soft deletion and reopening.
2. Call POST /auth/memberUser/join to create a new member user and obtain their access token.
3. As this member, call POST /todoApp/memberUser/todos with an ITodoAppTodo.ICreate payload to create a new active todo and capture todoId.
4. Using the member token, call DELETE /todoApp/memberUser/todos/{todoId} to logically delete the todo. Confirm from the response (or a follow-up GET /todoApp/memberUser/todos/{todoId}) that deleted_at is non-null and state reflects a removed or equivalent state according to the lifecycle rules.
5. Still authenticated as the same member, call PUT /todoApp/memberUser/todos/{todoId}/reopen to attempt to restore the deleted todo.
6. Assert that the operation succeeds, the response ITodoAppTodo shows deleted_at is now null, state is set to an active/pending value, and updated_at is advanced while id and created_at remain unchanged.
7. Optionally, verify through search or direct retrieval that the reopened todo is now returned in member-visible lists and is no longer treated as deleted.

Key business validations:
- Reopen correctly reverses logical deletion when allowed, clearing deleted_at and resetting state.
- Ownership is enforced: only the member who owns the todo can reopen their deleted item.
- No new todo record is created; the same id is reused and lifecycle timestamps behave consistently with a restore operation.
- System settings do not prevent valid reopening even if they limit active todo counts, unless explicitly configured to do so.

scenario.draft:
Ensure that calling the reopen endpoint on a todo that is already in an active state behaves idempotently and does not corrupt lifecycle fields or produce inconsistent state, while returning a successful result or an appropriate business-rule response as defined by requirements.

Scenario outline:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join followed by POST /todoApp/adminUser/systemSettings to guarantee that the environment is correctly configured for normal todo creation.
2. Call POST /auth/memberUser/join to create a member user context and obtain an access token.
3. As this member, create a new todo via POST /todoApp/memberUser/todos with ITodoAppTodo.ICreate, ensuring the initial state is active/pending and that deleted_at and completed_at are implicitly null.
4. Without completing or deleting the todo, immediately call PUT /todoApp/memberUser/todos/{todoId}/reopen using the same member's token.
5. Capture the response and assert one of the allowed behaviors defined by business rules, typically:
   - The endpoint succeeds but leaves state, completed_at, and deleted_at unchanged (purely idempotent no-op), or
   - The endpoint responds with a conflict or validation-style error explaining that only completed or deleted todos may be reopened.
6. If the operation is defined as idempotent success, verify that updated_at may advance but that state remains active and that no new record is created. If defined as an error, verify the error code and message conform to documented error handling.
7. Optionally, call GET /todoApp/memberUser/todos/{todoId} afterwards to confirm that the todo's persisted representation matches expectations for an active item.

Key business validations:
- Reopen on an already active todo does not create duplicates or move the todo into an invalid state.
- Lifecycle timestamps and state remain consistent with the concept of idempotent state transition.
- Authorization is enforced so only the owner member can call reopen on their todo, even when it is already active.
- Error or success behavior aligns with documented lifecycle rules for allowed state transitions.

scenario.draft:
Confirm that a member user cannot reopen a todo owned by another member user, enforcing strict ownership-based authorization for the reopen lifecycle operation.

Scenario outline:
1. Call POST /auth/adminUser/join and POST /todoApp/adminUser/systemSettings to ensure system configuration for todo lifecycle is initialized.
2. Call POST /auth/memberUser/join to create Member A and obtain Member A's access token.
3. As Member A, call POST /todoApp/memberUser/todos to create a todo and then PUT /todoApp/memberUser/todos/{todoId}/complete to mark it completed, establishing a todo that belongs to Member A and is eligible for reopen by its owner.
4. Call POST /auth/memberUser/join again to create Member B and obtain a separate access token for this second member user.
5. Using Member B's token, attempt to call PUT /todoApp/memberUser/todos/{todoId}/reopen on the todo that belongs to Member A.
6. Assert that the response indicates an authorization failure (for example, 403 Forbidden or 404 Not Found depending on error-handling strategy) and that the todo's state, completed_at, and deleted_at remain unchanged when later read by Member A.
7. Optionally, as Member A, call GET /todoApp/memberUser/todos/{todoId} to confirm that the todo is still in the completed state and has not been reopened by Member B.

Key business validations:
- Ownership enforcement: only the member who owns the todo can perform reopen on it.
- Cross-account access to reopen other users' todos is blocked and does not leak sensitive existence information beyond what error-handling policy allows.
- The failed reopen attempt leaves the underlying todo record unchanged in todo_app_todos.
- Audit or session behavior, if implemented, continues to treat the unauthorized attempt as a normal error path without side effects on the todo lifecycle.

Authorization provider, decorator, and payload themselves compile, but global config import breaks overall build since MyGlobal depends on it and auth code imports MyGlobal.
authorizations.solution_guidance: Create a MyConfiguration.ts module in the same directory as MyGlobal.ts exporting the expected configuration shape (e.g., MyConfiguration interface or object), or adjust the import in MyGlobal.ts to point to the correct existing configuration module. Ensure the exported members match what MyGlobal.ts expects (types and values) so that all references resolve. If only types are needed, you can export appropriate interfaces/types; if runtime values are used, export a concrete configuration object. After adding this module or fixing the path, re-run the TypeScript compiler to confirm TS2307 is resolved.

2. Ensure MyGlobal.ts imports from './MyConfiguration' and that the imported symbol names match the exports.
3. Keep MyGlobal.ts API surface unchanged so all existing authorization providers and decorators (like adminuserAuthorize and AdminuserAuth) continue to compile without modification.

import { Controller, Ip } from "@nestjs/common";
import { TypedRoute, TypedBody } from "@nestia/core";
import typia from "typia";
import { postAuthGuestUserJoin } from "../../../providers/postAuthGuestUserJoin";
import { postAuthGuestUserRefresh } from "../../../providers/postAuthGuestUserRefresh";

import { ITodoAppGuestUser } from "../../../api/structures/ITodoAppGuestUser";

@Controller("/auth/guestUser")
export class AuthGuestuserController {
  /**
   * Register a new todo_app_guestusers guestUser concept and issue initial
   * ITodoAppGuestUser.IAuthorized tokens.
   *
   * This operation registers a new guest user concept in the
   * todo_app_guestusers table and issues initial authorization tokens for the
   * guestUser actor. The underlying Prisma table todo_app_guestusers is
   * designed to represent unauthenticated visitors, with an id field as the
   * primary key and optional metadata fields. When this endpoint is called, the
   * service will create a new row with a generated id and timestamps in
   * created_at and updated_at, optionally using the provided external_ref to
   * correlate with external analytics or tracking systems.
   *
   * From a security perspective, this endpoint is intentionally public
   * (authorizationActor is null) because guest users do not yet have any
   * credentials or authenticated identity. However, the service must implement
   * rate limiting and abuse prevention at an infrastructure level, as repeated
   * creation of guest concepts could be used for resource exhaustion. The
   * external_ref field, when supplied, should be validated as a bounded-length
   * string to avoid log pollution or injection issues.
   *
   * On the database side, the todo_app_guestusers table stores external_ref as
   * a nullable string, created_at as a non-null timestamp of when the record is
   * created, and updated_at as a non-null timestamp updated whenever the record
   * is modified. This API operation will populate created_at and updated_at
   * with the current server time when inserting the new guest concept row. The
   * id field is generated as a UUID, guaranteeing uniqueness across all
   * guestUser records.
   *
   * The business logic for this operation does not create any todos or
   * sessions; guest users in this system never own todo_app_todos records and
   * do not have dedicated session tables. Instead, the returned
   * ITodoAppGuestUser.IAuthorized payload will embed token information (such as
   * accessToken and refreshToken properties defined in the DTO) associated with
   * the created guest id, allowing subsequent token-based access to other
   * public or guest-limited endpoints.
   *
   * Validation rules include ensuring that external_ref, if provided, conforms
   * to any length or format constraints defined in the
   * ITodoAppGuestUser.IJoinRequest DTO and matches the semantics described for
   * external_ref in the todo_app_guestusers schema: an optional reference or
   * correlation identifier. The system should also ensure that timestamps are
   * generated server-side and not taken from client input. If insertion fails
   * due to database errors, the API must return an appropriate 5xx error with a
   * generic message while logging details internally.
   *
   * This operation is typically used at the beginning of guest journeys as
   * described in the requirements, where an unauthenticated visitor first
   * interacts with the todo service and needs a transient identifier for
   * analytics or feature gating. Related operations in the same authentication
   * workflow are the guestUser refresh endpoint, which renews tokens based on a
   * valid refresh token, and various public read-only endpoints that accept the
   * guest's access token to personalize or track usage without associating
   * persistent personal data.
   *
   * @param connection
   * @param body Guest join request payload containing optional external
   *   reference or metadata necessary to create a todo_app_guestusers record
   *   and establish an authorized guestUser context.
   * @setHeader token.access Authorization
   *
   * @nestia Generated by Nestia - https://github.com/samchon/nestia
   */
  @TypedRoute.Post("join")
  public async join(
    @Ip()
    ip: string,
    @TypedBody()
    body: ITodoAppGuestUser.IJoinRequest,
  ): Promise<ITodoAppGuestUser.IAuthorized> {
    try {
      return await postAuthGuestUserJoin({
        body,
      });
    } catch (error) {
      console.log(error);
      throw error;
    }
  }

  /**
   * Refresh guestUser authorization tokens based on a valid refresh token,
   * returning ITodoAppGuestUser.IAuthorized.
   *
   * This operation refreshes authorization tokens for the guestUser actor by
   * validating an incoming refresh token and issuing a new
   * ITodoAppGuestUser.IAuthorized structure. The underlying guest concept is
   * stored in the todo_app_guestusers table, which tracks the guest's id as a
   * UUID along with optional external_ref and the created_at and updated_at
   * timestamps. While guest users do not authenticate with passwords or
   * credentials, their tokens must still be strongly validated to prevent
   * unauthorized token reuse or token theft.
   *
   * From a security standpoint, this endpoint requires a valid refresh token
   * but is otherwise open in terms of actor identity, so authorizationActor is
   * set to null and the guard layer will rely on the refresh token validation
   * logic instead of a pre-established session. The refresh token is mapped to
   * a specific todo_app_guestusers.id, and the service must ensure the token
   * has not expired, has not been revoked, and matches the current guest state.
   * Any invalid token usage should result in an appropriate 401 or 403 error
   * response without revealing sensitive details.
   *
   * On the database layer, the todo_app_guestusers table itself does not store
   * tokens; instead, it provides a stable guest id that can be embedded in
   * tokens or used to look up associated data in other subsystems. The
   * updated_at field may be updated when a refresh occurs to reflect the last
   * time the guest concept was actively used, which helps with data lifecycle
   * and retention policies described in the requirements. The external_ref
   * field remains unchanged during refresh and continues to serve as an
   * optional correlation identifier.
   *
   * The request body for this operation is defined by
   * ITodoAppGuestUser.IRefreshRequest, which encapsulates the refresh token and
   * any additional metadata needed for validation, such as client identifier or
   * token family details. The response body must be
   * ITodoAppGuestUser.IAuthorized, following the naming rules for authorization
   * responses based on the TodoApp service prefix and the guestUser actor, and
   * will include newly issued access and refresh tokens along with guest
   * context fields.
   *
   * This operation is a core part of the guest authentication flow for the todo
   * service, typically called after the guest has initially obtained tokens
   * through the /auth/guestUser/join endpoint. Client applications should use
   * this refresh endpoint before access tokens expire to maintain a seamless
   * guest experience. If refresh fails due to invalid or expired tokens, the
   * client may need to call the join endpoint again to obtain a new guest
   * identity, depending on the business rules defined for guest lifecycle.
   *
   * @param connection
   * @param body Guest token refresh request containing the refresh token and
   *   related metadata required to validate and renew guestUser authorization.
   * @setHeader token.access Authorization
   *
   * @nestia Generated by Nestia - https://github.com/samchon/nestia
   */
  @TypedRoute.Post("refresh")
  public async refresh(
    @TypedBody()
    body: ITodoAppGuestUser.IRefreshRequest,
  ): Promise<ITodoAppGuestUser.IAuthorized> {
    try {
      return await postAuthGuestUserRefresh({
        body,
      });
    } catch (error) {
      console.log(error);
      throw error;
    }
  }
}
